About me

A developer from Chattogram who learns by shipping real projects.

I’m Asmit Sarkar, an aspiring full-stack and Android developer from Chattogram, Bangladesh. I finished my HSC in Science in 2026 from Sir Ashutosh Government College, and I’m currently focused on learning programming and coding, with a growing interest in cyber security.

On the Android side I build with Kotlin and Jetpack Compose — including DoremanAI, a voice-controlled personal assistant, and SUST OR DIE, a study-planner app I built to organise my own study routine. On the web I work with Python + Flask and Next.js: my Password Leak Checker and Expense Splitter are both live and used by real people.

My rule is simple: don’t just learn it — build it, ship it, and let people use it.

split.pyPython · Expense Splitter
# settle up a group in as few transfers as possible
def settle_up(balances):
    # balances: {member: net} — positive means "is owed money"
    owes = sorted((m for m in balances if balances[m] < 0),
                  key=lambda m: balances[m])
    owed = sorted((m for m in balances if balances[m] > 0),
                  key=lambda m: -balances[m])
    return match_transfers(owes, owed)  # e.g. B -> A 300, C -> A 300

01

Password Leak Checker

FeaturedWEB · LIVE

Checks whether a password or email has appeared in known data breaches, and rates password strength — the lookup never stores what you type.

✓ Privacy by design — nothing you type into this checker is ever stored.

PythonFlaskBreach APIs
Case study — problem, build & outcome
Problem
People reuse the same password everywhere and have no quick way to tell whether it has already leaked in a breach.
Built
A Flask backend that queries breach data through external APIs and rates password strength — nothing typed into the checker is ever stored.
Outcome
Live and public on Vercel — anyone can run a check right now from the Open Website button below.
Why this stack
Python + Flask — the job is one focused lookup: take a check, ask the breach data, send the answer back. A small Flask backend does exactly that, with nothing extra in the way.
Hard part
The checker asks for the most sensitive thing a person can type, so it had to be useful without keeping any of it. The fix is in the design, not in a setting: nothing typed into the checker is ever stored — the check runs, the answer comes back, and nothing is written down.
Trade-off
Storing nothing means there is no history to go back to — every check stands on its own. That is the deliberate price of the privacy design: privacy first, convenience second.

02

Expense Splitter

FeaturedWEB · LIVE

Splits group expenses fairly: create a group, add members and shared costs, and see exactly who owes whom — with 50 currencies to choose from, picked per group.

✓ Verified test — a 900 expense split three ways settles as exactly two transfers of 300.

PythonFlaskSQLiteChart.js
Case study — problem, build & outcome
Problem
Group trips and shared flats end in messy who-owes-whom maths that nobody wants to work out by hand.
Built
Flask + SQLite behind it: groups, members and shared expenses, a settle-up algorithm that minimises the number of transfers, and a currency picked per group at creation from 50 Asian currencies.
Outcome
Live on Vercel and verified end-to-end: a 900 expense split three ways settles as exactly two transfers of 300.
Why this stack
Python + Flask with SQLite — groups, members and expenses are structured records, and the balances are worked out on the server, so a lightweight database behind Flask covers the whole job.
Hard part
The settle-up algorithm: a group's balances can tangle into many possible payments, and the goal is to clear them all in as few transfers as possible. It sorts who owes against who is owed and matches them off until every balance reaches zero — the split.py snippet in the Skills section above shows the shape of it, and the verified test in the Outcome row above is it working.
Trade-off
Minimising transfers means the settlements don't mirror who originally spent what — someone may end up paying a person they never borrowed from directly. The choice was fewer, cleaner settlements over a payment trail that follows every single expense.

03

DoremanAI

ANDROID · SIGNED RELEASE

A Siri-style, voice-controlled personal assistant for Android — talk to it and it acts: calls, messages, answers and everyday tasks, powered by AI gateways.

Current build is a signed release build.

KotlinJetpack ComposeVoiceAI
Case study — problem, build & outcome
Problem
Everyday phone tasks — calling, messaging, quick answers — mean tapping through apps; a voice-first assistant can do them hands-free.
Built
Kotlin + Jetpack Compose: common voice commands are handled on-device first, and open questions go to AI gateways the user configures with their own keys.
Outcome
Distributed as a signed release through the GitHub releases page.
Why this stack
Kotlin + Jetpack Compose, native Android — the assistant's jobs are phone jobs, like calls and messages, so it is built as a native app rather than a web page in a wrapper.
Hard part
Routing each request to the right place: simple commands should be handled instantly on the phone itself, while open questions need AI. Common voice commands are handled on-device first, and only open questions go out to the AI gateway.
Trade-off
Open questions run through a gateway the user configures with their own key — more setup than a built-in account, but the key and the choice of gateway stay the user's.

SUST OR DIE

ANDROID · SIGNED RELEASE

My personal study-planner app: a 60-day study plan with syllabus tracking, Focus Mode, custom alarms and deadline countdowns.

KotlinJetpack ComposeStudy planner
Case study — problem, build & outcome
Problem
My own study routine needed one place for the plan, the syllabus and the deadlines — scattered notes were not working.
Built
Kotlin + Jetpack Compose: a 60-day study plan with syllabus tracking, Focus Mode, custom alarms, deadline countdowns and an offline routine tab.
Outcome

Trade-off
It is built for one person's routine — mine — so it fits my plan exactly instead of trying to fit everyone. It is shared as a public signed-release APK download, and the source code stays private.

05

IELTS Pathway

WEB · LIVE

A 60-day IELTS preparation planner aimed at Band 7 — 10 hours a day with spaced revision built in, in both Bengali and English, with dark and light themes.

Next.jsTypeScriptBN / EN
Case study — problem, build & outcome
Problem
IELTS prep is usually a pile of disconnected resources — no day-by-day path that also schedules the revision.
Built
Next.js + TypeScript: a 60-day, 10-hour-a-day plan targeting Band 7 with spaced revision built in, in Bengali and English, with dark and light themes.
Outcome
Live and public on Vercel — the full 60-day plan is open to anyone from the Open Website button below.
Why this stack
Next.js + TypeScript — the plan is 60 days of structured content in two languages; TypeScript keeps that plan data typed and consistent, and Next.js serves it as a web app anyone can open.
Hard part
A day-by-day path alone isn't enough — revision has to be scheduled too, or it never happens. Spaced revision is built into the 60-day plan itself rather than bolted on, and the whole plan runs in both Bengali and English.
Trade-off
One fixed path — 60 days, 10 hours a day, aimed at Band 7. The structure that makes the plan followable also makes it demanding, and one size has to fit everyone who follows it.

Skill DNA

WEB · LIVE

A GitHub skill analyzer that turns a public GitHub profile into clear skill proof a recruiter can read — what you’ve actually built, not just what you claim.

GitHub APIWebAnalyzer
Case study — problem, build & outcome
Problem
Recruiters see claimed skills, not proof — a GitHub profile holds the proof, but it is hard to read at a glance.
Built
A web analyzer on the GitHub API that turns a public profile into a clear, readable summary of what someone has actually built.
Outcome
Live and public on Vercel — open it from the Open Website button below.
Why this stack
Built on the GitHub API — the proof of what someone has built already lives in their public profile, so the analyzer reads that public data instead of asking anyone to type in a list of claimed skills.
Hard part
A raw GitHub profile is hard to read at a glance. The work was turning it into a clear, readable summary of what someone has actually built — skill proof a recruiter can scan in seconds.
Trade-off
It can only show what is public — private work never appears in it, so the picture it gives is only as complete as the public profile behind it.

07

Asmit MCP Server

PYTHON · OPEN SOURCE

A public Python MCP server that gives AI tools a URL-checking tool — with SSRF protection built in, so a fetch can't be redirected onto an internal address.

✓ Version 0.1.0 — main branch CI green: 28 unit tests pass, ruff clean.

PythonMCPSSRF protection
Case study — problem, build & outcome
Problem
A tool that fetches URLs on request has to be careful about where those URLs actually lead — a link can redirect somewhere internal that was never meant to be reached.
Built
A public Python MCP server (version 0.1.0) that exposes a URL-checking tool, with SSRF protection built in: the IP is pinned and re-verified at every redirect step, so a fetch can't be steered to an internal address.
Outcome
Public on GitHub at version 0.1.0 — main branch CI green, with 28 unit tests passing and ruff clean.
Why this stack
Python — the server's job is small and focused: take a URL check, guard the fetch, report back. Python keeps that job direct, and the project is held to a checked standard — 28 unit tests and ruff, both green in CI on the main branch.
Hard part
SSRF protection that survives redirects: checking an address once is not enough, because a URL can redirect — and each redirect can point somewhere new. The IP is pinned and verified again at every redirect step, so the check holds all the way through the fetch, not just at the start.
Trade-off
Pinning and re-verifying the IP at every redirect step is stricter than a single check up front — the protection wins over the shortcut: safety on every hop, even when it means more checking per fetch.

Architecture

How the pieces fit, end-to-end.

LAYER 01 — CLIENT

What the user touches

  • Android — Kotlin + Jetpack Compose UI
  • Web — Next.js / HTML pages in the browser
  • Responsive, phone-first layouts
→

LAYER 02 — LOGIC & API

Where the work happens

  • Flask routes & REST-style endpoints
  • External APIs — breach data, AI gateways
  • Business logic: splits, checks, planners
→

LAYER 03 — DATA & SHIPPING

Where it lives

  • SQLite for app data (Expense Splitter)
  • Code on GitHub, every project public
  • Deployed on Vercel for live web apps

Same shape in both live web apps: Password Leak Checker sends a lookup to its Flask backend, which queries breach data and answers — nothing typed is stored. Expense Splitter keeps groups and expenses in SQLite behind Flask, and works out the balances on the server.

Workflow

Six steps, in order — the same loop every project on this page went through.

Discover

Plan

Design

Develop

Test

Deploy

// one loop, every project — first idea to live link

01

Discover

Start from something real — a leaked password, a messy group bill, my own exam routine. If the problem isn’t real, I don’t build it.

02

Plan

Decide the smallest version that is actually useful, and the stack that fits it — Kotlin for Android, Flask or Next.js for the web.

03

Design

Lay the screens out phone-first, because my own Android phone is the screen everything has to work on.

04

Develop

Write it in small pieces, committing to GitHub as it grows, until the whole flow works end to end.

05

Test

Run it on a real phone with real data, then fix what breaks — including the bugs only real use turns up.

06

Deploy

Ship it live on Vercel or as an APK, share the link, and keep improving from what comes back.
